notes: Dev-split TBox revision (12 queries). The class rule is the definition of a Type II supernova (core collapse of a massive star; Wikipedia's lead), held by every model, with no real exception: the lightest progenitors (electron-capture supernovae) are still stars of 8 to 10 solar masses. The revision swaps the progenitor for a brown dwarf, a counterfactual that crosses a physical boundary (a brown dwarf never ignites hydrogen), which README allows. The derived queries name real but little-known Type II supernovae in the prompt (the membership is the bridge, stated) and ask what exploded (inheritance, 2 hops); the third is an application (what to look for in archival images). Changed in review: the earlier members (SN 1999em, SN 2013ej, SN 2004et) are well studied, and their progenitors are discussed by name (SN 2004et's and SN 2013ej's were found in pre-explosion images as supergiants; Wikipedia gives SN 1999em's progenitor mass), a stored per-member route that a TBox rule edit leaves open. They were swapped for SN 1968D (NGC 6946), SN 1961I and SN 1964F (both M61): supernovae from before progenitor searches, with no progenitor identification, whose type is known from their host galaxy's list. Original answers name the accepted alternative ("a massive star (such as a red supergiant)"): the usual expert answer for a Type II-P progenitor is a red supergiant ("progenitor was a red supergiant": 53 Dolma hits), which is a massive star, so the judge should read either as the original. The new answer was chosen so the near unrelated query (Type Ia: a white dwarf) differs from it and catches an edit that spreads to supernovae in general. has_progenitor is in staging/physics.RELATIONS.md. Main records/physics has no supernova-class TBox record (its SN 2011fe records are ABox constellation facts).
